# Status

Each feature is listed as built, mocked, planned or cut, with the tracks it serves.

- Built: records how it was verified, as the flow, the result, the date and the commit.
- Mocked: says what is faked and what the real version would need.
- Cut: keeps its line, with the reason.

- Cut: Revolut mispricing check with real data. Recomputes the source's airport figures from published prices, audience counts and attention studies, with attention seconds and the Meta price as sliders. Serves G-Research. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
- Cut: airport placement ranking per startup. Ranks UK and EU airport placements by how well each airport's route and airline mix matches the startup's target customer, with published or estimated prices and a sent enquiry; two startups are compared side by side in the demo. Serves G-Research and Wordsmith. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
- Built: onboarding form and results page, in `web/`, with live audience scoring and competitor research. Placement pricing remains mocked. The form is a fill-in-the-blank passage, "Our company is … in …. We want to reach … who would pay $… per …, and we can spend $… a month on ads in …", ending in a city menu whose only city is New York; all five boroughs are mapped without being listed. The results are a map of New York's census tracts with Customers and Competitors tabs, a Gap tab once qualifying campaigns are found, a legend and clickable campaign markers at matched stations, addresses and approximate areas. Each marker shows its competitor's logo, loaded from the competitor's own website, and falls back to initials when the site's icon cannot be fetched; each campaign row in the Competitors tab shows the same logo. Solid markers identify current or recent campaigns with a station or address match; dashed markers identify approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Markers open no popups: hovering a campaign marker highlights its row in the Competitors tab, clicking it switches to that tab and scrolls to the row, and clicking a row's location moves the map to the marker. Each mapped row shows the data-source attribution. The placements to buy are numbered markers that match their numbers in the list, shown on the Gap and Competitors layers. Without a Gap tab they also show on the Customers layer, where they are listed; with one, the Customers layer omits them. They are chosen from observed gaps when locations of campaigns from the past 12 months are available, or from audience fit otherwise. Hovering a placement on the map or in the list highlights it in both, clicking a row moves the map to it and, on phones where the map sits above the column, scrolls back up to the map, and clicking a marker scrolls the list to its row. Tabs above the results column pick the layer for both the map and the column, in the order Customers, Competitors, Gap. Gap appears only once a campaign from the past 12 months has a station or address match. Customers opens at the start; when Gap appears it opens by itself unless another tab was clicked. Switching tabs slides the highlighted tab across, and the map's colours change at once. The column shows only that layer's sections: Gap has the 5 biggest observed gaps and up to 12 placements to buy, Customers has the 5 tracts with the most target customers, the up to 12 placements when there is no Gap tab, and the weighted tract columns, strongest first, with those that count against the customer marked "less likely", and Competitors has the competitors, each with its logo on the right of the row, and their ads, with the agent's latest step while it searches a note counting ads without a reliable location match and so absent from the map, and a separate note counting ads that run across the city or a borough. Ads with no fixed location are labelled citywide or borough-wide on their row, and the map's legend counts citywide campaigns as not pinned. Hovering a tract on the map names it and shows the current layer's value for it, and hovering a trait under Customers shows its exact weight in place of its measure. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Add hover values to tract boxes and trait bars`: web lint, typecheck and build passed; the hover tooltips were not checked in a browser. On the form, the whole background spins once every 30 seconds, sweeping colour through the edges the form card leaves visible, and its four coloured blobs each drift on their own loop of 7 to 10 seconds, moving up to 50% of the screen's larger side and growing by up to 40%. Submitting the form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds while the same spin and drift play 12 times faster, so the background turns at 144 degrees per second, with the form visible behind it until the movement finishes. The speed-up continues from the background's current position rather than restarting, and Edit returns it to normal speed. Reduced-motion preferences stop the spin and drift and skip the visible movement. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up the form background during the results transition`: the spin went from 25 degrees to 29 at the click with no jump, then turned about 65 degrees in the next 400 milliseconds; all five animations ran 12 times faster during the slide and returned to normal after Edit; screenshots 10 seconds apart on the form showed the red and yellow moving from the bottom-left corner to the bottom centre; the browser had no console errors, and web lint, typecheck and build passed. Earlier, on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up gradient rotation during results transition`, desktop and 390-by-844 mobile checks showed a 1.2-second slide with no horizontal overflow. The results fill the window: the map fills the left two thirds and stays in view while the column scrolls in the right third, and on phones the map sits on top at 55% of the screen height. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Animate results upward after form submission`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks confirmed that the results and their content move together, settle at the top without horizontal overflow, and preserve the form answers on Edit. Reduced motion completed immediately, invalid amounts blocked submission, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The column opens with a one-line summary of the brief and an Edit button that brings the form back with its answers kept. Submitting a completely empty form runs the sample dating-app brief with an $8,000 monthly budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown keeps full required-field and numeric-pattern validation. A button at the bottom left, opposite the settings gear, opens three briefs tested with live research (dating app, budget gym, dinner delivery) and fills the form with the chosen one. There is no separate `/map` route. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use sample defaults for empty form submissions`: a blank submission showed the sample map and 12 placements; each individually filled field and a changed payment dropdown blocked incomplete submission; numeric patterns still blocked invalid amounts; a complete custom brief submitted its own values and Edit kept them; `/map` returned 404. The browser had no console errors, and all 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. The sample brief changed to the dating app on 8 November 2026; its recorded run holds five competitors and twenty ads, nine with map locations, and the blank-form flow was not re-checked in a browser after the change. Verified on 8 November 2026 for the example-briefs button: web lint and typecheck passed and the button renders in the server HTML; opening its panel and prefilling the form were not checked in a browser. Faked: placement costs, minimum spends are invented. Real: the audience fit scores are weighted sums of the real scaled tract columns, and the placements are real kiosks and shelters selected across eligible tracts in descending observed gap-score order when campaigns from the past 12 months have precise locations, or descending audience fit otherwise, with one per tract and at least 500 metres between them. The column weights come from Jev through AI Gateway when `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is set in `web/.env.local`, or on a Vercel deployment through its OIDC token: one request asks a five-level score question per column, from strongly against to strongly for, and each weight runs from -1 to 1, the probability-weighted level. Without either, or when Jev fails or takes over 20 seconds, the weights come from keyword matching on the target customer, and the Customers tab says so. Verified on 8 November 2026 with the sample brief: the Customers tab said "weighted by Jev", and the scoring request, Jev plus the tract arithmetic, took 892 ms. For "young professionals in tech who rent with roommates", the strongest weights were jobs in information (+0.94), residents aged 20 to 34 (+0.89) and median age (-0.83). Jev isn't on AI Gateway's free tier, so the key's Vercel team needs purchased AI Gateway Credits, and a card Vercel can verify. The browser computes competition per tract from its distance to each current or recent campaign's matched station or street address, falling to about a third at 1 km, and the gap as audience fit times one minus competition; that formula is a first version, not a decision. The UI imports audience scoring, streamed competitor research and placement lookup through `web/src/lib/api.ts`, with types in `web/src/lib/contract.ts`. Placements appear after audience scoring and are re-ranked when research finishes. On 7 November 2026, the live energy-drink flow returned three competitors and three source-linked campaign findings. Their dates or station locations were unknown, so none lowered the gap scores. The production sample fallback showed three recorded competitors and its capture-date label; a different brief received no recorded findings. Both browser flows had no console errors. Verified in `2a85115`. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Show competitor logos in the list and on campaign markers`: web lint, typecheck, build and all 32 tests passed, and the logo endpoint returned a PNG for each of the sample run's three competitors. The logos were not checked in a browser. Serves G-Research and HRT.
- Built: a settings menu (gear button, bottom right) with experimental interface options saved in the browser: sharp corners (every border radius 1px), percentile classes on or off (on paints four classes above the 50th percentile and leaves the bottom half clear; off is the earlier smooth ramp), a cost-estimate switch (on by default; shows the invented price per customer, sorts placements by it and tags the lowest; off shows no prices and lists by area), and a colour palette. Classic is selected by default and listed first. Night mode has a moon button in the header and a switch in the settings menu. Every palette has a dark version, so the chosen colours carry over, and the map switches to CARTO's dark basemap. The app follows the operating system's light or dark preference until someone chooses a mode, then remembers that choice in the browser, and the settings menu can return it to following the system. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Add night mode with a dark variant for each palette`: web lint and typecheck passed and the app and the deck rendered in the server HTML; neither light nor night mode was checked in a browser. The teal and coral palette is ink text (#12211F, #5B6B69, #8A9694) on #FAFAF8 with #E3E8E7 dividers, a teal ramp (#BFE0DC #7FC2BA #2F8F86 #0B5450) and a coral accent (#F2603D, darker #C9431F); teal appears only in the map fill, the active layer tab and the legend bar. Teal and coral, blue and lime, purple and amber, and a colour-blind navy palette are the alternatives. Placement markers are 24px accent circles with a white ring, 30px and darker when selected, and merge into numbered groups when they overlap at the current zoom; the map frames the placements when they first arrive. Most customers lists the five neighbourhoods with the most tracts in the top 3%, with tract counts. Verified on 8 November 2026 in headless Chrome. Not an agreed product decision, only options to compare.
- Built: competitor research with the Vercel AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent`, OpenAI directly through `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and hosted web search and page reading. The research default is `gpt-5.6-luna`, selected in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`. Model names are not read from environment variables. Research runs in two stages. Discovery finds up to six competitors from the startup's product and target customer rather than its industry label: the model first writes short shopper phrases for the product and customer, then searches at least four times, recent campaign news first, for companies that have run New York subway, billboard, bus shelter, LinkNYC or wild-posting campaigns and that sell a substitute or target the same customer. Government campaigns, non-profits and media owners are excluded. Discovery also records every campaign its searches turn up, including ones that name no place, using recent campaigns and the current year in its searches. It cannot finish with fewer than three competitors until it has made five searches. Discovery has twelve model steps and a 60-second deadline. Each competitor then gets its own placement search for stations, street addresses, neighbourhoods and dates, told which campaigns are already recorded, with eight model steps and 65 seconds, all running concurrently within a 165-second total deadline; the Route Handler has a 170-second deadline. One finding can name up to six places, and each place becomes its own row. Each competitor can contribute up to six rows with a map location and three without, counted separately so that findings without a place cannot crowd out located ones. A run reports at most 54 rows. The first model step of each stage requires hosted search, and each response allows up to eight hosted tool calls, in parallel. Typed tools reject URLs absent from the run's research sources. Hosted-search-only responses continue into reporting within the same step budget. The model extracts the evidence; source membership does not independently fact-check its summary. Dates are classified as current, recent, historical or unknown. Current needs a date range covering today. Recent needs a source showing the campaign running within the past 12 months, using its start date, end date or latest evidence date. The agent may use a publication date as the latest evidence date only when the source reports the campaign as launching or running then, and a date given only as a month or year counts as the first day of that period. Only matched subway stations or street addresses with current or recent dates affect competition. Geocoded areas and unknown or historical dates remain visible as markers without lowering gap scores. Other findings stay visible with source links, evidence and locations. A search returning no campaigns does not establish that competitors are absent. The sample recording contains four competitors and twelve campaign findings, five of them with map locations, one of them recent at a street address so the recorded fallback can open the Gap tab. The Competitors tab ends with a "How the agent worked" section: the tools the agent called with counts (web search, open page, report competitor, report campaign, locate on map, and the two finish tools), then its reasoning summaries and each call in order, grouped by phase or competitor; the section folds away from its heading. Reasoning comes from OpenAI's `reasoningSummary: "auto"` and from the notes the model writes before searching; recorded research has no trace. Re-capture it from `tools/` with `uv run python -c 'from tools.sources.competitor_run import load; load(refresh=True)'` while the web app runs. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Count campaigns from the past 12 months as competition`: in the browser, the dating-app brief classified Hinge, The League and HER as running in the past 12 months, and The League's billboard at 41st Street and 7th Avenue, reported on 16 October 2026, made the Gap tab appear with the recent-advertising wording. The budgeting-app brief, with no recent campaign at a precise location, kept audience fit in that browser run, and a live run of the same brief through the API qualified a StreetEasy placement at Thompson Street and West Houston Street. The browser had no console errors from the app. All 49 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Verified earlier, on 8 November 2026 in commit `Record campaigns during discovery and pin named neighbourhoods`: three live runs across two briefs took 37 to 62 seconds. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop, and its Openigloo marathon campaign produced approximate markers at Fort Greene, Williamsburg, Greenpoint, Park Slope and the Upper East Side. The dating app found Hinge, The League, Tinder, Plenty of Fish and HUD, with 18 campaign findings, 10 of them on the map. None of the findings had confirmed current dates, so none lowered gap scores. In the browser, the sample brief showed the rows and the map note with no console errors. All 49 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Verified earlier, on 8 November 2026 in commit `Find competitors from the product and customer, then search each for placements`: live runs of four briefs each completed in 27 to 43 seconds. The dating app found Plenty of Fish, Hinge, The League, Bumble, Cerca and HUD, with 12 campaign findings, four of them at matched subway stations. The budgeting app found Openigloo, StreetEasy and Job Today; the pizza delivery service found Slice, Seamless and WoodSpoon; the telehealth service found Roman. None of the findings had confirmed current dates, so none lowered gap scores. In the browser, the sample brief listed Openigloo, StreetEasy and RentHop with seven campaign findings and no console errors. All 32 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. In a scratch comparison over 12 test briefs, searching named direct competitors found no campaigns at a named station or street address for any brief, and this two-stage search found them for 10 of 12. Verified earlier, on 7 November 2026 in `2a85115`: live research and production fallback flows above; eight focused tests for CSV parsing, source checks, station matching, dates, gap effects, split SDK stream chunks, interruption and cancellation; HTTP 400 for invalid briefs and 413 for oversized briefs; web lint, typecheck and build; Python Ruff checks; station data and recording present in the production deployment trace. Serves G-Research. Search and page reading alone do not establish the browser-control workflow for Wordsmith.
- Planned: verified placement prices and minimum spends, and competitors' stores and offices as separate presence evidence. Serves G-Research and HRT. Browser control remains unbuilt for Wordsmith.
- Built: shared model and provider setup in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, using the installed SDK provider registry. Code defaults select OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` for research and Gateway Jev for audience decisions. The research adapter bundles the model, search tool, options, credential checks, source decoding and provider errors. Unsupported research providers are rejected until a compatible search adapter is added. Model environment variables have no effect; `.env.example` lists credentials only. GPT-5.6 Luna selection was verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use GPT-5.6 Luna for competitor research`: all 13 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. A live smoke test returned competitor findings and streamed search progress. Verified on 7 November 2026 in `f0e401d`: all 13 focused tests passed, including registry resolution, model-environment independence, credential separation, source decoding and unsupported research-provider rejection. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. In the browser, the sample showed "weighted by Jev" and completed research with no verified competitors and no console errors while the old model variable was set to an invalid value. Serves G-Research and HRT.
- Built: campaign location lookup with Geoapify, using `GEOAPIFY_API_KEY` on the server, and street corners from a table of New York intersections. Supported source-reported landmarks, neighbourhoods and street addresses are resolved within New York. A neighbourhood gets an approximate marker at the neighbourhood itself. Geoapify results that are only the borough, a business named after the area, or a street that shares the area's words are rejected, because it returned Brooklyn itself for "Fort Greene, Brooklyn", a veterinary clinic for "Upper East Side, Manhattan" and a Bronx street for "West Village". Street corners, written as "A and B", "A & B", "A at B", "corner of A and B" or "A between B and C", are looked up in `data/streets/intersections.csv`, 55,978 intersections built by `tools/src/tools/sources/streets.py` from NYC Open Data's street centerline, and get address precision. A corner found in several boroughs is placed only when the text names one of them or a neighbourhood in it, and a corner not in the table stays unmapped; neither is sent to Geoapify, whose free-text search returned Madison Avenue & East 41st Street for "41st Street & 7th Avenue". A location naming only a borough stays unmapped. When Geoapify finds nothing for a place followed by its borough, such as "Times Square, Manhattan", it is asked again for the place alone. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Place street-corner campaigns from the city's street centerline`: 54th Street and Broadway, 14th Street and Franklin Street in Williamsburg, Sixth Avenue at Carmine Street, Lafayette and Prince Streets, and Lafayette Street between Spring and Kenmare Streets all resolved to the right corner; "41st Street and 7th Avenue" without a borough stayed unmapped; all 36 tests, web lint, typecheck and build, and the Python Ruff checks passed. Most campaign findings remain unmapped because their sources say only that the campaign ran across the subway, with no station or street. Reliable station and address matches carry their precision; broad landmarks are labelled approximate. Citywide and borough-wide campaigns are labelled as having no fixed location and get no marker, because no single point represents them. Weak results, ambiguous alternatives and outside-city results stay unmapped with an explanation. Successful results are cached for 24 hours per server process, up to 500 entries. An unavailable key, rejected key, timeout or lookup failure preserves campaign evidence. Markers appear for known locations regardless of dates, with dashed styling for approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Clicking a marker opens the Competitors tab at its row, which shows its source, date status, location precision and attribution. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Focus campaign rows from map markers instead of popups`: with a pizza-delivery brief, clicking DoorDash's approximate Brooklyn marker from the recommendations tab switched to Competitors and highlighted its row, and clicking the row's location flew the map to the marker; the browser had no console errors, and lint, typecheck and build passed. Only current or recent campaigns with station or street-address matches affect competition and gap scores. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Map campaign landmarks with Geoapify`: the live key resolved Times Square as approximate; the health-and-wellness flow returned Finch's Times Square billboard and displayed its undated marker and source popup on desktop and at 390 by 844 pixels. No geocoding requests appeared in browser network traffic, no API-key query strings appeared in the page, and there were no browser console errors. All 22 focused tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Serves G-Research.
- Built: geographically spaced placement recommendations. The selector follows the supplied tract ranking: descending observed gap scores when campaigns from the past 12 months have precise locations, or audience fit otherwise. It allows at most one site per tract and requires at least 500 metres between every pair. It searches beyond the top 15 tracts to fill up to 12 slots, returning fewer if eligible sites run out. Within a tract, invented cost remains the tie-breaker; advertising eligibility and mocked budget limits still apply. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Spread placement recommendations across gap areas`: the live AI-meeting-notes brief for large enterprises with a $50,000 monthly budget returned 12 placements in 12 tracts, with a minimum separation of about 518 metres and descending gap scores. The browser had no console errors. All 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed, including tests for cross-boundary spacing, alternative sites, lower-ranked tracts and eligibility filters. Serves G-Research and HRT.

- Built: structured campaign searches, research outcomes and audience-only recommendations. The competitors tab distinguishes completed, partial, failed and timed-out research, counts searches and source URLs, reports source rejections, and separates historical, date-unconfirmed and unmapped findings. Without campaigns from the past 12 months at precise locations, recommendations and their legend explicitly use audience fit, and the competitors map leaves tract colouring off. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Improve campaign research and handle unknown coverage`: the live sample completed five searches across two competitors with no campaign findings and showed audience-only recommendations. The energy-drink brief completed eight searches across two competitors and returned three source-linked campaign findings, two with approximate map locations. It reported one rejected source and one unmapped campaign; none established current coverage, so recommendations kept audience fit. Browser fixtures covered complete-empty, failed, timed-out, historical and current evidence; only current precise evidence enabled Gap. Desktop and 390-by-844 mobile checks had no horizontal overflow or console errors. All 32 tests, web lint, typecheck and build passed. Serves G-Research and HRT.
- Built: pitch deck at `/presentation` in `web/`, made with Spectacle and loaded in the browser only. It has five slides with speaker notes: cover, problem, how it works, live demo and next steps. It uses the app's CSS variables and its three fonts, and follows the app's palette and night mode. The live demo slide embeds the app's form page in an iframe, laid out at 1.4 times the frame's size and scaled down so the form and its submit button fit. An Export PDF button, shown on hover in the top-right corner, opens Spectacle's export view with every slide on its own 1366 by 768 page and opens the print dialog once fonts load. Backgrounds print even with the dialog's background graphics option off. Serves the pitch for every track. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Add Spectacle pitch deck at /presentation`: web lint, typecheck and build passed; every slide was checked in a browser in light mode and the next steps slide in dark mode; presenter mode showed the cover's notes; a PDF printed from the export view had five pages with full-bleed backgrounds and no buttons; the console showed no errors or warnings. The print dialog itself was not opened, and the demo flow inside the iframe was not run.

1: # Audience heatmap
2: 
3: Status: chosen, 7 November 2026.
4: 
5: ## Idea
6: 
7: A startup fills in the same short form as the [ad channel mispricing finder](ad-channel-mispricing.md): industry, the startup in one sentence, the target customer in one sentence, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It gets back a heatmap of a city showing where its target customers live, work and pass through, where competitors already advertise to them, and the gap between the two. The run ends with specific placements to buy in the strongest gap areas. The demo city is New York.
8: 
9: It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.
10: 
11: ## Origin
12: 
13: Raised by Viktor on 7 November 2026 as a pivot from the ad channel mispricing finder. That idea needed prices for advertising placements, which are mostly unpublished, while public data about where people live, work and travel is plentiful. The competition and gap layers, the competitor-campaign agent and the closing list of placements were suggested by an agent in the same conversation, and the user accepted them.
14: 
15: ## How it works
16: 
17: Decided on 7 November 2026; the decisions are in [product.md](../product.md).
18: 
19: 1. Input: the onboarding form above. The target customer sentence becomes weights on census and trip data, such as age, income, industry and household type. Jev, a decision model, scores how strongly the sentence implies each attribute.
20: 2. Audience fit layer: each area of the city is scored by how many target customers live there, work there or pass through it.
21: 3. Competition layer: a browser agent finds the startup's competitors, then searches press, trade sites and social media for their outdoor campaigns in the city, such as "<competitor> subway ad" or "<competitor> billboard NYC", and places each find on the map. Where it finds nothing, competitors' stores and offices stand in.
22: 4. Gap layer: areas with high audience fit and low competition. This is the default view; the other two layers are toggles that explain it.
23: 5. Placements: specific placements a startup can buy inside the strongest gap areas, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member and a way to measure it (a QR code, promo code or landing page). Budget filters out placements with minimum spends.
24: 
25: An hourly view of the audience fit layer, using subway and taxi data by hour, is an open option, not a decision.
26: 
27: ## Evidence and data
28: 
29: Checked on 7 November 2026 by querying each source's API or download index. "Checked" means we fetched the column list, a sample row and the row count or file list. "Fetched" means a source module in `tools/src/tools/sources/` downloads it and writes the processed output named. The New York open data portals (data.cityofnewyork.us and data.ny.gov) list no licence on these datasets.
30: 
31: Who lives where:
32: 
33: - US Census Bureau American Community Survey, 5-year estimates for 2024 (fetched): the `census` source writes `data/census/nyc_tracts.csv`, one row for each of New York City's 2,327 census tracts (an area of about 4,000 people). Columns: population, median age, median household income, per capita income, and the shares aged 20 to 34, with a bachelor's degree or higher (of those aged 25 and over), with household income of $150,000 or more, and enrolled in college. Median household income is missing for 128 tracts and is capped at $250,001 by the Census Bureau. The API needs a key, read from `CENSUS_API_KEY` in `tools/.env`.
34: - Census Bureau 2024 cartographic boundary file for New York State's tracts (fetched): the `tracts` source writes `data/tracts/nyc_tracts.geojson`, 2,324 tract shapes clipped to the shoreline. Three tracts in the Census table have no shape in this file.
35: 
36: Who works where:
37: 
38: - US Census Bureau [LODES](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/ny/) (job counts by home and work location), version 8: files for New York State run to 2024. Workplace files count jobs per census block by earnings band and industry, and origin-destination files link home and work blocks. They show daytime audiences, such as finance workers in Midtown. Fetched: the `lodes` source sums the 2024 workplace file for all job types to tracts and writes `data/lodes/nyc_tract_jobs.csv`, 2,305 tracts and 4.84 million jobs. Columns: jobs, and the shares of jobs held by workers aged 29 or younger, paying more than $3,333 a month, and in each of eight sectors (information, finance and insurance, professional services, education, health care, retail, arts and recreation, and accommodation and food). A degree share is also kept, but LODES reports education only for workers aged 30 and over, so it is the share of those workers.
39: 
40: Who passes through:
41: 
42: - [MTA Subway Hourly Ridership: Beginning 2025](https://data.ny.gov/d/5wq4-mkjj) (checked): 47.4 million rows, updated 4 November 2026. Each row is one station complex, one hour and one fare class, with ridership, transfers, latitude and longitude. The fare class category, such as full fare or student, gives a rough audience signal. Earlier years are in separate datasets (2017 to 2019, and 2020 to 2024). Fetched: the `subway` source averages the four weeks from Monday 5 October to Sunday 1 November 2026, one day per query because longer queries time out, and writes `data/subway/stations.csv` (428 station complexes with weekly riders and the share on each fare class) and `data/subway/hourly.csv` (average riders per station, weekday and hour). The "Students" fare class covers school students' fare cards and "Fair Fare" is the city's discount for low-income riders.
43: - [Pickups and Drop-offs by Taxi Zone and Industry](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/c5iv-bn4s) (checked): monthly counts per taxi zone for yellow taxis, green taxis and high-volume ride-hail companies, with data to September 2026. [Taxi zone shapes](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/8meu-9t5y) are a separate dataset.
44: - TLC [trip record files](https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/tlc-trip-record-data.page) (file list checked): monthly Parquet files to September 2026 for yellow taxis and high-volume ride-hail. Fares and tips per trip could serve as a rough income signal; the columns were not checked.
45: - [Citi Bike trip data](https://s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata/index.html) (file list checked): monthly files to October 2026, under Citi Bike's [data sharing policy](https://www.citibikenyc.com/data-sharing-policy), which was not read.
46: - [Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/cqsj-cfgu) (checked): only 114 locations, mostly retail corridors and bridges, counted in May and September or October for morning, midday and evening, from 2007 to May 2026. Too sparse for a citywide layer; useful to check the other layers at those points.
47: 
48: Where ads can be bought:
49: 
50: - [LinkNYC Kiosk Locations](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/s4kf-3yrf) (checked): 2,255 sites with address, coordinates and census tract. By kiosk type: 2,032 live Link1.0 kiosks, 151 live Link5G kiosks marked "Ad", 57 live Link5G kiosks marked "NonAd", and a few removed or payphones. Only the Link5G types say whether they carry ads; whether Link1.0 kiosks do is unchecked. Fetched with the bus shelters by the `placements` source, which keeps live kiosks only.
51: - [Bus Stop Shelters](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/t4f2-8md7) (checked): 3,312 shelters with coordinates and neighbourhood, updated 1 October 2026. The data has no field saying whether a shelter carries advertising. The `placements` source writes kiosks and shelters to `data/placements/nyc_placements.csv` (5,556 rows), with carries_ads set to yes, no or unknown.
52: - Joined per tract (fetched): `tools.analyze` writes `data/analysis/nyc_tracts.csv`, one row per tract with its Census columns, its LODES job columns, the subway station complexes within 1,300 feet (about a five-minute walk) and their weekly riders, and its counts of LinkNYC kiosks, kiosks marked as carrying ads, and bus shelters. The tract shapes, with only geoid and borough, go in `data/analysis/nyc_tracts.geojson` so the browser loads them once. 1,373 tracts have a station nearby and 125 contain a kiosk marked as carrying ads. The 21 columns that audience fit can weight also appear scaled from 0 to 1 as their percentile rank across the city. A tract missing a value gets 0.5. The 81 tracts with no residents get 0 on resident columns, and the 19 with no jobs get 0 on job columns; both keep their subway score. The same run writes `data/analysis/columns.json`, listing those 21 columns with a description of each and whether it measures where people live, work or pass through. It also writes `data/analysis/nyc_placements.csv`, the 5,556 kiosks and shelters each with its tract. Startup-specific scoring and the competitor campaigns are added in the web app, not in these files.
53: - [DOB Sign Application Filings](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/nyis-y4yr) (checked): 15,288 filings, but only from April 2013 to October 2017. It covers all signs, not only advertising, and gives an address and tax lot rather than coordinates. Not usable as a current billboard map.
54: 
55: Competitors:
56: 
57: - Competitors' outdoor campaigns: no public list exists, so the agent in step 3 gathers them from press, trade sites and social media.
58: - Competitors' stores and offices: OpenStreetMap or a places API. Not checked.
59: 
60: ## Existing products
61: 
62: No search has been run yet. From memory: foot-traffic and audience-mapping products such as Placer.ai already map where audiences go, and AdQuick offers audience modelling for outdoor advertising. The audience heatmap differs by mapping one startup's customer from a one-sentence description, adding a layer of competitors' actual outdoor campaigns, and ending with placements to buy. Without the competition layer it would be close to products that already exist.
63: 
64: ## Tracks it could serve
65: 
66: - G-Research: strong. The hidden things are where a startup's customers are and where competitors haven't reached them. They are found by combining public datasets with an agent's search for campaigns, and they tell the startup where to advertise, which covers the brief's three questions.
67: - HRT: moderate. Stronger with the hourly view, which would forecast when an area holds the most target customers and turn that into a buying decision.
68: - Wordsmith: moderate. The competitor-campaign agent is a multi-step browser workflow: find competitors, search several kinds of site, read the results and place each campaign. The rest of the product is data processing, not browser work.
69: - Bank of Scotland: weak. It serves startups, not consumers' cost of living.
70: - Metaview overall prize: a city heatmap is a strong visual demo.
71: 
72: ## Challenges it could use
73: 
74: - Gemini API: the competitor-campaign agent, if it runs on a Gemini model.
75: - Tiger Data: hourly ridership and trip data are time series, which fits the hourly view if it is built.
76: - Vultr: hosting the data processing or the demo.
77: 
78: ## Open problems
79: 
80: - Licences: the New York open data portals list none on the datasets checked, and Citi Bike's data sharing policy has not been read.
81: - Billboards have no current public map. The only sign dataset stops in 2017, so the placements step relies on LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, and on shelters only if we can find which ones carry advertising.
82: - The competitor-campaign agent may find few campaigns for small competitors, leaving the competition layer mostly made of stores and offices, which show where competitors are, not where they advertise.
83: - Some target customers, such as "developers at Series A startups", have no direct census field, so Jev's weights may describe them poorly. Jev was checked only on "young professionals in tech who rent with roommates", where its weights matched the sentence.
84: - The competitor agent's design is open: which model it runs on through AI Gateway, whether it searches with a search API or reads pages in a headless browser, how a campaign found in an article is matched to a station (station names in the text, or geocoding addresses), and how long it may run. One run is estimated at 30 seconds to 2 minutes, unmeasured.
85: - The web app asks for placements only after the agent finishes, because placements come from the gap. With a real agent, the placement list could stay empty for up to 2 minutes. Showing placements from audience fit first and re-ranking them when the agent finishes, or capping the agent at a time budget such as 45 seconds, would avoid that.
86: - With few campaigns, the gap layer looks almost the same as audience fit. Each campaign lowers the gap only within about 2 km of its station, so the stand-in's five stations change an estimated 5% of the city's area, a rough figure from the reach around five points, not a measurement. Competitors' stores and offices as a fallback would widen the competition layer.
87: - What a customer pays is collected by the form and meant to stand in for lifetime value in the audience weighting, but nothing uses it yet, and how it should change the scores is undecided.
88: - Prices for LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters are probably unpublished, so cost per audience member would be an estimate. How to estimate it is undecided.
89: - Judges in Edinburgh may ask why New York. The answer is that New York publishes the most data and the method works elsewhere, which the pitch should say up front.
90: - The mispricing claim of the earlier idea, and the Revolut evidence behind it, no longer support the product directly. The pitch needs its own evidence that competitors leave gaps in a city.
91: 
92: ## Scope
93: 
94: New York only, with its data gathered ahead of time by scripts in `tools/`. Demo one startup end to end: the form, the gap map with the audience fit and competition layers as toggles, the competitor campaigns the agent found, and the placements to buy in the top gap areas. A recorded run of the competitor agent is kept as a fallback in case the live agent fails.
95: 
96: ## Alternatives
97: 
98: - [Ad channel mispricing finder](ad-channel-mispricing.md): the idea this replaces. It ranked specific placements, last narrowed to airports, by cost per attentive second weighted by audience value, but most placement prices are unpublished. It shares the onboarding form and the aim of reaching customers competitors miss.

# Docs

Rules for writing files under `docs/`.

## Writing

- Do not coin abbreviations, acronyms or capitalised names for project concepts. Use the term already in the codebase, or a plain description, because invented shorthand cannot be searched for later.
- Define a term the reader cannot look up in half a sentence at first use. This matters most for names the document coins itself, since they exist nowhere else.
- Describe what code does and under what conditions. Do not assert importance with a metaphor in place of the mechanism.
- Lead with the answer, so a reader who stops after the first sentence still has it.
- One idea per paragraph, carried by its first sentence.
- Headings name their content, such as "Why the request times out", not "Analysis".
- Short, active sentences. Split anything past roughly thirty words unless splitting reads worse.
- Never drop a fact, quantity or qualifier to read more simply. Plain wording is the goal; less precision is not. This protects facts about the subject, not superseded statements about it.

## Correcting existing docs

- Before correcting a document, search all of it for statements the change makes false. If the search finds any beyond the passage being edited, list them with line numbers in the reply. Fixing only the passage you happened to read is the usual failure.
- Replace each false statement in place. Delete what is now wrong rather than writing around it.
- What changed, and why the old text was wrong, goes in the reply, not the document.
- The result must read as if written today from scratch. A reader who has never seen the previous version cannot tell which parts changed.
- The exceptions are the history these rules ask for: a changed decision in `product.md` is updated in place with its new date, and a dropped or merged idea keeps its file with the reason.

## Event docs

`docs/event/` summarises the original sponsor and MLH material in `reference/`.

- `tracks.md` has one section per sponsor track and `challenges.md` one per MLH challenge, each under a heading, with no summary tables.
- A section that draws on material in `reference/` names that file on its "Source" line.
- To add new material, store the original in `reference/tracks/<sponsor>/` or `reference/mlh/`, then summarise it into the matching section. Keep the original's facts, quantities and deadlines; plan decisions belong in `product.md`, not here.

## Product docs

Agents keep these current without being asked.

- `product.md` says what the product is, who it is for and what sets it apart. Its Decisions section records every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who it serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect and the demo scope. Each is one line with the decision, reason and date, and a changed decision is updated in place. Never record a suggestion the user has not accepted. Track and challenge priorities live in the root `AGENTS.md`, not here.
- `status.md` lists each feature as built, mocked, planned or cut, with the tracks it serves. A built feature records how it was verified: the flow, the result, the date and the commit. A mocked feature says what is faked. A cut feature keeps its line with the reason. A change to code or demo data means re-checking the claims it affects.
- `pitch/notes.md` holds internal pitch notes. `pitch/judges/` holds only what judges will see, one file per track named after the sponsor, such as `judges/jetbrains.md`.

## Track groups

`track-groups.md` records which sponsor tracks one project can enter together and which MLH challenges fit any project. Idea files can link to its groups instead of repeating the reasoning. It is analysis, not a decision; update it when `event/tracks.md` or `event/challenges.md` changes.

## Ideas

`ideas/` holds candidate product ideas from brainstorming, one file per idea, named in kebab case after the idea (`ad-channel-mispricing.md`). An idea is not a decision. Idea files are not among the shared files that need approval in the root `AGENTS.md`.

- Record an idea only after it has been explored and the user agrees to record it. This holds whether the user, a teammate or an agent raised it. An idea counts as explored once its track fit, open problems and demo scope have been discussed, which is what its file needs. At that point, ask the user whether to record it.
- Origin says who raised the idea, including when an agent did.
- When an idea is compared with another, link to the other's file rather than describing it inline. If the other has no file yet, describe it briefly and offer to record it once it has been explored.
- When the user chooses an idea, set its status to chosen and record the decision in `product.md`. When an idea is dropped or merged into another, set its status and reason; never delete the file, because the reasons stay useful.
- Judge track fit against the judging notes in `event/tracks.md`, not the track title alone.

Each idea file uses these sections, in this order. Sections marked optional appear only once there is something to put in them.

1. Title, then a status line: `Status: proposed`, `chosen`, `dropped` or `merged into <file>`, with the date and, for dropped or merged, the reason.
2. Idea: what it does and for whom, in a short paragraph.
3. Origin: who proposed it and what prompted it. Source material goes in Evidence and data.
4. How it works (optional): the inputs, the steps the product takes, what it outputs, and any calculation or model it relies on. This is the product design; what the demo shows goes in Scope.
5. Evidence and data (optional): sources that support the premise, with their dates and how reliable they are, and the data the product needs, with whether access has been checked.
6. Existing products (optional): outside products and research that already cover part of the idea, how this idea differs, the date of the search, and what the search did not cover.
7. Tracks it could serve: each track with strong, moderate or weak, and why.
8. Challenges it could use: each MLH challenge whose technology fits a part of the idea, and which part.
9. Open problems: unverified assumptions, unchecked data access, and risks. Facts already found go in Evidence and data or Existing products, not here.
10. Scope: what a 24-hour demo would show, end to end.
11. Alternatives: links to the idea files it was compared with, and how it differs. Outside products go in Existing products.

# Product

## What it is

The audience heatmap shows a startup where in a city its target customers live, work and pass through, and where it can find evidence of competitors' outdoor advertising. A startup fills in a short form about its product, customer, budget and markets. It gets back a map of the city with audience fit, competition evidence, and placement recommendations. Recommendations use observed gaps when campaigns from the past 12 months have precise locations; otherwise they use audience fit and state that competition coverage is unknown. The run ends with specific placements to buy, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member and a way to measure results. The demo city is New York.

It is for startups that want customers beyond Meta and Google but have no media agency and a limited budget.

Three things set it apart from audience-mapping products and outdoor ad marketplaces:

- It maps one startup's target customer, described in a sentence, rather than a fixed set of audience segments.
- It gathers evidence of where competitors have advertised, using an agent that searches the web and reads campaign pages. Areas without verified campaigns have unknown competition coverage.
- It ends with placements a startup can buy in those areas, not just a map.

## Decisions

Every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who the product serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect, and the demo scope. Track and challenge priorities are recorded in `AGENTS.md`, not here. One line each: the decision, the reason, and the date. A changed decision is updated in place, so this section always describes the current plan.

- Product idea: the audience heatmap, which maps where a startup's target customers live, work and pass through in a city and where competitors leave them unreached; details in `ideas/audience-heatmap.md`. It replaces the ad channel mispricing finder (`ideas/ad-channel-mispricing.md`), keeping its onboarding form, because public data about people and places is far richer than published prices for advertising placements. 2026-11-07.
- Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint) managed with pnpm, in the `web/` folder rather than the repo root. The repo root stays for docs and agent config, and a second service such as a Python API can sit beside `web/` later. 2026-11-07.
- Frontend UI: shadcn/ui components styled with Tailwind CSS v4. 2026-11-07.
- LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK in the web app. Jev uses Vercel AI Gateway. The competitor-campaign agent uses OpenAI directly through `@ai-sdk/openai` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`, as chosen by the user on 2026-11-07. The Python scripts in `tools/` call no language model. Python prepares the numerical dataset, and everything that depends on one startup's form runs in the web app. 2026-11-07.
- AI model configuration: model defaults live in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, so switching models requires one code edit and no model environment variables. The defaults are `openai:gpt-5.6-luna` for competitor research and `gateway:typesafe-ai/jev` for audience decisions. The user selected GPT-5.6 Luna for research on 2026-11-07. The Vercel AI SDK provider registry resolves both. The research adapter keeps its model, hosted search tools, provider options, credential checks, source decoding and error messages together. Audience scoring resolves a decision model separately. Environment variables supply credentials only. 2026-11-07.
- Audience fit scoring: Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision model, scores the target-customer sentence against each column of the prebuilt tract dataset, and the web app weights the columns by those scores. Jev answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text, and is called as `typesafe-ai/jev` through AI Gateway. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so Jev's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. One request costs about $0.00001. 2026-11-07.
- The onboarding form asks for industry, a one-sentence description, a one-sentence target customer, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. The form reads as one sentence, "Our company is … in …. We want to reach … who would pay $… per …", which fits shops, services and B2B companies as well as startups, and describes customers the company wants rather than ones it has (2026-11-08). Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.
- Submitting the completely empty onboarding form runs the sample dating-app brief for a dating app for people looking for a serious relationship, targeting single professionals in their late twenties and thirties who live in Manhattan and Brooklyn, at $30 per month and an $8,000 monthly advertising budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown requires the complete form. The sample uses the main form flow so it needs no separate `/map` route. The brief replaced the fintech budgeting app on 2026-11-08, because live runs of the fintech brief found no competitors or ads, while the dating brief found four competitors and twelve ads, five of them with map locations. 2026-11-08.
- The form page has an example-briefs button at the bottom left, opposite the settings gear, which opens the three briefs tested with live research and fills the form with the chosen one: the dating app, a budget gym and a dinner delivery app. Picking an example again applies it again. The empty-form sample stays the dating app. It exists so the rehearsal can switch briefs without retyping them. 2026-11-08.
- Submitting the onboarding form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds, so the transition shows the new view arriving over the form. The background gradient rotates steadily at 150 degrees per second behind it until the results cover the form. Reduced-motion preferences skip the visible movement. 2026-11-08.
- Product name: Placewise, shown in the web app's header. The form's markets field is a city menu whose only city is New York, with a disabled "more cities coming" entry, so the demo presents New York as the first of several cities. The form maps all five boroughs without listing them. 2026-11-08.
- Demo city: New York, because it publishes the most detailed public data on residents, workers, trips and advertising locations. The method is meant to work in any city with similar data. 2026-11-07.
- Map markers open no popups. Clicking a placement or campaign marker highlights and scrolls to its row in the results column, switching to the Competitors tab for a campaign, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08. Popups drew beneath placement markers and repeated what the column already shows.
- The output is one map with audience fit, competition evidence, and recommendations. It has two tabs, Customers and Competitors, until a campaign from the past 12 months has a station or address match. A third tab, Gap, then appears and ranks high audience fit with low observed competition. Gap opens by default once it exists, unless the user has already picked another tab. Without a Gap tab, the Customers tab lists the placements, chosen by audience fit and labelled as not confirmed gaps. Without qualifying evidence, the Competitors view shows campaign markers without colouring tracts as low competition. Missing evidence remains unknown coverage. This keeps useful recommendations without presenting audience fit as a verified advertising gap, and without a third tab that would repeat the Customers ranking. Decided by the user on 2026-11-08.
- Map: MapLibre GL through react-map-gl, on CARTO's light Positron basemap. MapLibre recolours every tract from one paint setting when the layer changes, and react-map-gl is maintained by the team behind deck.gl; CARTO's basemap needs no API key and is run by a company, where OpenFreeMap, the other keyless option, has one maintainer. The browser loads the tract shapes from a Route Handler that serves `data/analysis/nyc_tracts.geojson`, so the data keeps one copy in `data/`. 2026-11-07.
- Competitor research uses the Vercel AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent`, with OpenAI web search and page reading, as chosen by the user on 2026-11-07. Competitors are the companies already advertising outdoors in New York to the same customer: discovery searches from the startup's product and target customer, not its industry label or named direct rivals, and keeps companies that sell a substitute or target the same customer, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08. Searching named direct rivals rarely finds campaigns, because small rivals seldom buy outdoor advertising, and the industry label alone returns unrelated mass-market brands. The code separates competitor discovery from each competitor's placement search, so repeated searches for one brand cannot consume another brand’s budget. Discovery has twelve model steps and 60 seconds and reports three to six competitors. It also records every campaign its searches turn up, including ones that name no place, because earlier searches saw far more sources than they reported. It prefers recent campaigns, searching recent campaign news first and adding the current year to its queries, including the placement stage, which also looks for stated run dates, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08, after four live briefs returned campaigns dated 2016 to 2024 only. Each then gets eight model steps and 65 seconds to search for stations, street addresses and dates, running concurrently within a 165-second total deadline. Each competitor can contribute six rows with a map location and three without, counted separately so that vague findings stay as a fallback without crowding out specific ones, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08. One finding can name several places, each becoming its own row. The model reports competitors and campaigns through typed tools. No public campaign list has been identified. Source links must appear in that run's research results. Findings keep their evidence, locations and known dates. All reliably located findings have map markers, including historical campaigns and unknown dates. Only campaigns that are current, or that a source shows running within the past 12 months, with a matched station or street address affect the heatmap; approximate areas do not. The 12-month rule was decided by the user on 2026-11-08, because sources rarely publish end dates. A campaign counted this way may no longer be up, so the Gap tab describes recent advertising rather than current coverage. Research outcomes distinguish completion, partial results, failure and timeout, with search counts, source URLs found, rejected source submissions and competitor completion counts. Findings without mapped locations or evidence from the past 12 months remain visible but do not count as competition. Missing evidence means unknown coverage. Stores and offices remain planned as separate evidence of competitor presence, not proof of advertising. 2026-11-08.
- Campaign geocoding: Geoapify, using `GEOAPIFY_API_KEY` on the server, as confirmed by the user on 2026-11-07. This places billboards and other campaigns without forcing a subway-station match. Street corners, such as "41st Street and 7th Avenue, Manhattan", are never sent to Geoapify, because its free-text search returns a different corner with full confidence; they are placed from a table of New York street intersections built from NYC Open Data's street centerline, decided on 2026-11-08. A corner that exists in more than one borough is placed only when the source names the borough or a neighbourhood in it. Lookups are restricted to New York; broad landmarks such as Times Square and neighbourhoods are labelled approximate. A campaign whose source names a place gets a marker there. A campaign that names only the city, a borough or the transit network gets no marker and is labelled as having no fixed location, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08, because any point on the map would claim a presence no source supports. Successful lookups are cached for 24 hours in each server process, up to 500 entries. The map does not credit Geoapify, as decided by the user on 2026-11-08; Geoapify's terms require that credit only on its free plan. Each mapped campaign's row in the Competitors tab retains the data-source attribution, such as OpenStreetMap, which the terms require on every plan. Dates and location precision are separate: an undated or approximate campaign can be shown without being counted as current competition. 2026-11-07.
- Each run ends with up to 12 specific placements to buy, such as LinkNYC kiosks and bus shelters, each with an estimated cost per audience member. Recommendations follow descending observed gap scores when campaigns from the past 12 months have precise locations, or descending audience fit otherwise, with at most one placement per tract and at least 500 metres between placements. The search continues through lower-ranked tracts when candidates are missing or too close, so one cluster cannot fill the list. A map alone is something audience-mapping products already offer, and a placement is something a startup can act on. 2026-11-08.
- Superseded on 8 November 2026 by the user: placements no longer carry a way to measure them (a QR code, promo code or landing page), because the options were invented and gave no information. Originally: every recommendation came with one, because marketers avoid channels they can't measure. 2026-11-07.
- Superseded on 2026-11-07 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports: Demo scope: confirm the Revolut airport mispricing with real data, by checking the source's figures (cost per thousand impressions and per thousand attentive seconds against Meta, and the breakeven attention) against published prices, audience counts and attention studies. The source's model rests on assumptions, so the aim is to test them. 2026-11-07.
- The web app runs each startup's result live when the form is submitted, so a startup typed in at the demo gets its own map. Only the city dataset is prepared ahead of time. Jev and the agent run in Node.js inside the web app, so no Python runs behind it. 2026-11-07.
- How the web app's server does the work: a Server Function takes the form, reads the tract data and column list from `data/`, calls Jev, and returns an audience fit score per tract ID. The browser loads the tract shapes once, not on every submission. The competitor-campaign agent runs in a Route Handler that streams typed events with `createUIMessageStream` and `createUIMessageStreamResponse`. The browser uses `DefaultChatTransport` and `readUIMessageStream` to decode them. A Server Function returns only when it finishes, and Next.js runs a client's Server Functions one at a time. The server matches explicitly named subway stations and uses Geoapify to locate source-reported landmarks and street addresses. Ambiguous, citywide, weak or outside-city matches remain unmapped with an explanation. The data stays in `data/`, and `outputFileTracingRoot` and `outputFileTracingIncludes` in `next.config.ts` include the analysis, station table and recorded research in the deployment. 2026-11-07.
- What the Python analysis writes for the web app, all in `data/`: the street intersections used to place campaigns at street corners, the tract shapes, and a tract table with each feature column also scaled from 0 to 1 so weighted columns can be added; a column list giving each column's name, a plain description and whether it measures living, working or passing through, from which the web app builds its Jev questions; the placements with their tract; and the subway stations. 2026-11-07.
- The Python scripts are one library module per data source, each with a `load()` that returns its data and downloads it first only if nothing is cached, plus one analysis entry point that imports them, joins them per census tract and writes the city dataset the web app reads. Caching makes reruns fast and lets the demo work offline. 2026-11-07.
- Build order: the frontend is built first against stand-in server calls, and the real Server Function and Route Handler come once the frontend is mostly done. The stand-ins return the same types the backend will, from `web/src/lib/contract.ts`, so the UI does not change when they are swapped. 2026-11-07.
- New York data is gathered ahead of time with scripts in `tools/`. A recorded live run of the competitor-campaign agent is kept as a fallback for the sample brief. It is used only when live research fails before returning findings and the city, industry, product and target customer match the recording. Every results tab labels recorded research with its capture date. Other briefs never inherit the sample's competitors. The source module `tools.sources.competitor_run` captures a complete run from the running web app without calling a model directly. 2026-11-07.
- Competitor logos: each competitor's own website is recorded alongside its name, and the app shows the site's icon from DuckDuckGo's favicon cache, in the competitors list, on each of that competitor's campaign rows and on its campaign markers, because a name alone does not make a competitor on the map or in the ads list recognisable at a glance. A competitor without a usable site, or whose icon fails to load, shows its initials. The research agent reports the website, so no logo files or manual curation are needed. 2026-11-08.
- Pitch deck: a `/presentation` route inside the web app, built with Spectacle and themed with the app's existing CSS variables and fonts, with no new colours, so it matches the app in light and dark mode. Five slides, one idea each with speaker notes: cover, problem, how it works, live demo and next steps. The demo slide embeds the running app in an iframe, the deck loads in the browser only, and it exports to PDF through printing. 2026-11-08.
- Default palette: Classic is selected by default and listed first in the settings menu, and no palette is named Default; the former default is now Teal, coral, as decided by the user. 2026-11-08.
- Colour-blind palette: the settings menu offers a fifth palette, navy and amber, whose heat ramp darkens from light to dark instead of changing hue, so a reader who cannot tell the hues apart still ranks the tracts. The user asked for it on 2026-11-08, after analysis found that the existing four put their lightest heat colour at the middle of the ramp, which leaves the score dots in the rankings non-monotonic. That analysis also found the default palette's amber-to-red pair loses its hue distinction under protanopia and deuteranopia, where it survives only by lightness. The other four palettes stay as they are, and the settings menu labels this one "Colour-blind friendly" under its name. 2026-11-08.
- Night mode: a moon button in the header and a switch in the settings menu turn the app dark and back. Each palette has its own dark version, so the chosen colours carry over, and the map switches to CARTO's dark basemap. The app follows the operating system's light or dark preference until someone uses the button or switch, then keeps that choice in the browser; the settings menu can return it to following the system. The user asked for night mode on 2026-11-08 and chose a dark version per palette and system-following behaviour over one shared dark theme. 2026-11-08.

content.text:
Compared against `docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md` (How it works + Scope), most of it is built. What is still not done:

**Genuinely missing**
- **Competitors' stores and offices as the fallback when no campaign is found** (description step 3, last sentence). Status lists it as Planned, not built.
- **A browser agent** in the literal sense (description step 3 and the Wordsmith note). Research runs on OpenAI hosted web search and page reading, not browser control; "browser control remains unbuilt for Wordsmith" in `docs/status.md`.
- **Verified placement prices and minimum spends** — Planned; the UI shows invented prices and invented minimum spends (a mocked part of the built feature).
- **The market scan of existing products** (description line 62, "No search has been run yet"). Still true; it is analysis, not a feature.

**Deliberately dropped or changed, so the description is now stale**
- **"a way to measure it (a QR code, promo code or landing page)"** (step 5). Cut on 8 Nov in `product.md`: the options were invented and carried no information.
- **"This is the default view; the other two layers are toggles"** (step 4). Replaced on 8 Nov by two tabs, Customers and Competitors, with Gap appearing only once a campaign from the past 12 months has a station or address match and opening by itself then.
- **The hourly audience view** was always marked an open option, not a decision, so it is not missing.

Two smaller deviations are expected, not gaps: cost per audience member is mocked, and "pass through" uses subway ridership only — taxi/ride-hail and Citi Bike were only checked, never fetched, which matches how the evidence section labels them.

Want me to update `docs/ideas/audience-heatmap.md` so steps 3–5 stop describing the dropped measurement, the old default layer and the unbuilt stores/offices fallback as current?
